pixels/one: A classifier looks at a whole image and answers with one label: the name of a class, like tree.
pixels/every: To find where the tree is, every pixel needs its own label: sky, tree or ground. That is segmentation: it splits the image into segments, one per class.
pixels/shrink: A ConvNet cannot do that as it stands: its strided convolutions and pooling shrink a sixty four by sixty four image into an eight by eight grid.
pixels/deep: It grows deeper instead, to two hundred and fifty six channels: it knows what is in the image, but only roughly where. Each cell of its grid stands for an eight by eight patch of pixels.
pixels/fcn: In 2015, Jonathan Long, Evan Shelhamer and Trevor Darrell made a ConvNet label every pixel, with a layer that learns to grow the small grid back to full size. Growing a grid is upsampling.
pixels/grow: At full size, the last layer gives one channel per class, C of them: a score for each class at every pixel, shape C by sixty four by sixty four.
pixels/argmax: Each pixel's label is its arg max: not its highest score, but which class has it.
stamp/setup: The layer that grows is a transposed convolution. Take one row: an input, x, of one, two and three, and a filter, w: one, two, one.
stamp/first: Each input value stamps a copy of the filter, scaled by that value, into the output. The one stamps one, two, one.
stamp/next: The next stamp starts S places further on: S is the stride, here two. The two stamps two, four, two.
stamp/add: Where stamps overlap, they add: position two gets one, plus two. Three.
stamp/all: The three stamps three, six, three. Add it all up: one, two, three, four, five, six, three. Three numbers became seven.
name/gather: Why transposed? Run the same filter as an ordinary convolution, stride two, over seven numbers: each of its three outputs gathers a patch of three inputs.
name/spread: Reverse every connection, keeping its weight, and each input spreads into a patch of three outputs instead: the stamps.
name/matrix: As a matrix, M, the convolution has one row per output, each holding the filter, two places further along each time.
name/flip: Reversing the wiring turns its rows into columns: the transpose. Now each column, scaled by one input, is a stamp. Hence the name.
name/history: Vincent Dumoulin and Francesco Visin explained it this way in 2016. They argued against its older name, deconvolution, which would mean undoing a convolution: this restores only the size.
size/starts: How long is the output? Call the input's width W: here, three. The first stamp starts at zero, and each of the other W minus one starts S further on, so the last starts at S times W minus one: four.
size/width: Add the filter's width, F, which is three, and the output is seven long.
size/pad: Padding, P, runs backwards too: the convolution added P zeros at each end of its input, so this trims P off each end of its output. With P of one, seven becomes five.
size/formula: So the width is S times W minus one, plus F, minus two P.
size/undo: It is the convolution's size rule, run backwards. With a filter of four, stride two and padding one, a convolution halves thirty two into sixteen, and the transposed one doubles it back.
